title: How to Read (and Actually Enjoy) More Books this Year
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart argues that counting books read is a weak metric that quietly corrodes a teacher's reading life, and that clarity of purpose is what actually determines what reading yields. He recounts abandoning Goodreads-style tallies and lists three effects counting had on him: no detectable link between volume and wisdom, a mix of pride and goal-stress, and an unhelpful legalism about what counts as having read a book. He then turns the legalism question into a teaching analogy, comparing it to a teacher asking how to score every point on an evaluation rubric instead of thinking hard about the craft itself. The positive claim follows: how much enjoyment, wisdom and knowledge a reader gets depends on how clear the purpose of the reading is, compounded across tens of thousands of reading minutes over a decade. He anchors the claim in Adler and Van Doren's How to Read a Book, summarised as the rule that how we read should flow from why we read. The piece closes by trailing a follow-up on a non-freaked-out approach to reading as a teacher, with the hypothesis that clearer thinking about reading improves reading instruction too. It is best read as a professional-habits piece for teachers rather than a literacy-pedagogy piece.
points: Stuart distinguishes metrics that change behaviour usefully, such as money spent or miles run, from Number of Books Read, which he found had no clear effect on how wise or joyful he became.
The counting habit produced two specific harms he names: pride that makes humility impossible, and deadline stress that turns reading into a quota chase.
The what-counts-as-reading-a-book question is dismissed as legalism, and he parallels it with teachers optimising for every point on an observation rubric rather than getting better at teaching.
His central mechanism is compounding: small differences in purpose clarity, multiplied across tens of thousands of reading minutes over a decade, change who a reader becomes.
He roots the argument in Adler and Van Doren's formula that how we read should flow from why we read, and notes that most English teachers have never read that book.
quotes: But then I stopped keeping track of how many books I read — publicly and privately — and I don't think I'll ever go back. I can't tell you how many books I read in 2015 simply because I don't keep count.

Measuring the quantity of books that I read had no clear effect on how smart or wise or good at life or joyful I was. This isn't true for everything, but it's true for reading. When I measure how much money I make and spend, there's a clear effect on how wisely I use my money.

Since there's no detectable correlation between Number of Books Read and Degree to Which Life Has Improved, I think my mind created correlations. I got proud of reading the books; I thought of myself as smart. This is really dangerous from a whole bunch of perspectives.

I could be wrong, but I don't know of any great readers from the past who worried about this, just like I don't know of any great teachers of the past who've ask, “How do I get all the points on my evaluation rubric?” They are less interested in teacher evaluation rubrics than they are in thinking deeply and clearly about teaching itself, doing the thing better.

The degree to which we gain enjoyment, wisdom, and knowledge from our reading of books depends on how clear our purposes are. The clarity of purpose with which we read significantly affects what we get from a given reading, and if you multiply that difference by the tens of thousands of minutes you'll spend reading over the next decade or so, the difference in who you become grows exponentially.

I'm not alone in advocating for the power of purposeful reading — it's the central premise of Adler and VanDoren's 1972 classic How to Read a Book . In short, Adler and VanDoren spend a book saying this: how we read should flow from why we read .
